title: Modal Deduction: Present and Past
grammarTitle: Modal Verbs for Deduction — Present and Past
grammarNote: Модальные глаголы дедукции позволяют выражать уверенность в выводе на основе улик или доказательств. На B1 уровне важно понимать три уровня уверенности (must / might-may-could / can't) и уметь применять их как для настоящего, так и для прошлого через perfect infinitive.

grammarTable.subject: PRESENT: must be
grammarTable.example: "She must be tired." / "He must know about it." / "You must be joking."

grammarTable.subject: PRESENT: might/may/could be
grammarTable.example: "She might be at home." / "He could be right." / "They may be coming."

grammarTable.subject: PRESENT: can't be
grammarTable.example: "He can't be serious!" / "She can't be home — her car is gone."

grammarTable.subject: PAST: must have + pp
grammarTable.example: "She must have left already." / "He must have been exhausted."

grammarTable.subject: PAST: might/could have + pp
grammarTable.example: "She might have missed the bus." / "He could have overslept."

grammarTable.subject: PAST: can't/couldn't have + pp
grammarTable.example: "He can't have written this." / "She couldn't have finished already."

rows.example: "She must be tired — she's been working for 12 hours." (evidence forces conclusion) ✅
"He might be at the library. Or he could be in a lecture." (possibility, not certain) ✅
"She can't be the manager — she started this week!" (evidence makes it almost impossible) ✅

rows.form: must be ≠ have to be (different uses)
rows.example: "You must be Amir!" (deduction about identity) ✅ vs "You have to be here by 9." (obligation) ✅
"The results may indicate X." (formal writing) ≈ "The results might indicate X." (informal) ✅
"He could be right, but I'm not sure." (tentative) ✅
"She must have left before us — the door was already locked." ✅
"He might have missed the announcement — he was away." ✅
"She could have forgotten — she has a lot on her mind." ✅

rows.form: can't have + pp = almost impossible past
rows.example: "He can't have finished the whole report — he started it at 9." ✅

rows.form: couldn't have + pp = same as can't have
rows.example: "She couldn't have known about it — the information wasn't available." ✅

rows.form: must have been + V-ing = continuous past
rows.example: "She must have been waiting for a long time — she looked exhausted." ✅
"She must be sleeping — all the lights are off." ✅
"He might be waiting outside — I didn't see him in the room." ✅
"She must have been studying all night — she knows everything." ✅
"He might have been trying to contact you — check your missed calls." ✅
"He can't have been sleeping — I heard him moving around." ✅
✅ "She must have FORGOTTEN." — must have + past PARTICIPLE. "Forgot" = past simple. ✅
✅ "She MUST BE tired." — modal + base form. NEVER "must to be." ✅
✅ "He couldn't have KNOWN." — past participle of "know" = "known." ✅
✅ "She must have KNOWN." (simple perfect) OR "must have been knowing." ✗ → "must have been aware." ✅

rows.form: ✗ Using "must" for obligation AND deduction interchangeably
rows.example: "You must be right." (deduction ✅) ≠ "You must be here at 9." (obligation ✅) — different meanings!
"She must have left already." → "You're probably right. Her coat is gone." ✅
"She can't have left — her phone is still here." ✅
"She must be outside." → "Or she might have gone to the library." ✅
"He might have been delayed." (50%) → "He MUST have been delayed — it's 2 hours." (95%) ✅

grammarTip:
Modal Deduction — levels of certainty:

PRESENT:
must be = ~95% certain (positive)
might/may/could be = ~50% possible
can't be = ~95% certain (negative)

PAST (+ perfect infinitive):
must have + pp = almost certainly happened
might/could have + pp = possibly happened
can't/couldn't have + pp = almost certainly didn't

CONTINUOUS:
must be + V-ing / must have been + V-ing
might be + V-ing / might have been + V-ing

⚠️ Common errors:
✗ must to be → ✅ must BE
✗ must have forgot → ✅ must have FORGOTTEN
✗ couldn't have knew → ✅ couldn't have KNOWN

💡 must ≠ have to:
must be (deduction) ≠ must be here at 9 (obligation)

exercises.instruction: Present deduction — must, might, or can't?
exercises.text: "She knows every detail about the project. She ___ be the project manager."
exercises.hint: Strong evidence (knows every detail) → near-certainty. "She MUST BE the project manager." ✅

exercises.text: "He failed the exam. He ___ be disappointed."
exercises.hint: Failing an exam → near-certainty of disappointment. "He MUST BE disappointed." ✅

exercises.text: "She's speaking fluent Mandarin. She ___ be a complete beginner."
exercises.hint: Evidence (fluent Mandarin) makes "complete beginner" almost impossible. "She CAN'T BE a complete beginner." ✅

exercises.text: "She ___ (take) the wrong bus — she arrived two hours late."
exercises.hint: Past evidence → high certainty. "She MUST HAVE TAKEN the wrong bus." ✅

exercises.text: "He's not answering messages. He ___ (run out of) battery."
exercises.hint: One possible explanation (not the only one) → MIGHT HAVE. "He MIGHT HAVE RUN OUT OF battery." ✅

exercises.text: "He ___ (write) this report — he was in hospital all week."
exercises.hint: Evidence (in hospital all week) makes it almost impossible. "He CAN'T HAVE WRITTEN this." ✅

exercises.text: "She ___ (study) all night — she knows everything perfectly."
exercises.hint: Evidence → high certainty about ongoing past action. "She MUST HAVE BEEN STUDYING all night." ✅

exercises.text: "She must have forgot her keys."
exercises.hint: ✅ "She must have FORGOTTEN her keys." — "forgot" = past simple; need past participle "forgotten." ✅

exercises.text: "You must be Kamila!" — "must" here expresses:
opts: Obligation — you have to be Kamila
Deduction — I'm almost certain you are Kamila
exercises.correct: Deduction — I'm almost certain you are Kamila
exercises.hint: "must be X" when meeting someone = deduction about identity. "You MUST BE Kamila!" ✅

exercises.text: "He looks exhausted. He ___ (sleep) well last night."
exercises.hint: Evidence (looks exhausted) → near-certainty he didn't sleep well. "He CAN'T HAVE SLEPT well." ✅

exercises.text: "I don't know why he didn't come. He ___ (forget) about it, or he ___ (be) ill."
exercises.correct: might have forgotten / could have been
exercises.hint: Two possible explanations → might/could have. "MIGHT HAVE FORGOTTEN / COULD HAVE BEEN ill." ✅

exercises.instruction: Must be vs must have been — choose.
exercises.text: "She looks confused now. She ___ the explanation."
exercises.hint: She looks confused NOW = evidence of past failure to understand. "She CAN'T HAVE UNDERSTOOD the explanation." ✅

exercises.text: "She couldn't have ___ the answer — no one told her."
exercises.hint: "couldn't have KNOWN" — past participle of "know" = "known." ✅

exercises.text: In a formal academic paper: "The data ___ indicate that treatment is effective."
exercises.hint: "May" is slightly more formal than "might." In academic writing: "The data MAY indicate..." ✅

exercises.text: "The door is locked, the lights are off, and nobody is answering. They ___ out."
exercises.hint: Multiple pieces of evidence all pointing to same conclusion → strong deduction. "They MUST BE out." ✅

exercises.text: "He ___ (delay) — he's 10 minutes late." → Two hours later: "He ___ (delay) seriously — something is wrong."
exercises.correct: might have been delayed / must have been delayed
exercises.hint: 10 min: "MIGHT HAVE BEEN DELAYED" (50%). 2 hours: "MUST HAVE BEEN DELAYED" (95%). ✅

exercises.text: "The library was warm and there were empty coffee cups. Students ___ (study) there for hours."
exercises.hint: Evidence of ongoing activity (warm room, empty cups) → continuous. "Students MUST HAVE BEEN STUDYING there for hours." ✅

exercises.text: "She submitted the essay at 11:59 p.m. She ___ until the last minute."
exercises.hint: "MUST HAVE BEEN WAITING until the last minute" — the continuous form emphasises the duration of the waiting. ✅

exercises.text: Find the incorrect sentence.
exercises.hint: ✗ "can't have KNEW" — "knew" = past simple. ✅ "can't have KNOWN." ✅

exercises.text: "She won the competition." — Which deductions about her skill are valid?
exercises.hint: All three follow from the evidence (she won): must be talented ✅, can't be beginner ✅, might have practised ✅.

questions.hint: "Must be" for deduction = ~95% certain from evidence. ✅
must have + PAST PARTICIPLE. "forgotten" = pp of "forget." ✅

questions.text: "He looks completely lost. He ___ (understand) the instructions."
questions.hint: Evidence (looks lost) → near-certainty he didn't understand. "He CAN'T HAVE UNDERSTOOD the instructions." ✅

questions.text: "Couldn't have known" vs "can't have known" — difference?
opts: "Couldn't have" = past from the past; "can't have" = past from present
questions.correct: "Couldn't have" = past from the past; "can't have" = past from present
questions.hint: Both work. "Couldn't have known" = slightly more narrative. "Can't have known" = speaking from present perspective. ✅

questions.text: "She might have been waiting." — "might have been waiting" is:
questions.hint: "might have been waiting" = might + have + been + V-ing = modal deduction about ongoing past activity. ✅

questions.text: "You must be Amir!" vs "You must be here at 9." — difference:
opts: "Must be X" = deduction about identity; "must be here" = obligation
questions.correct: "Must be X" = deduction about identity; "must be here" = obligation
questions.hint: "must be X" (deduction) ≠ "must be at X at Y time" (obligation). Context determines meaning. ✅
"She MUST BE SLEEPING." — modal + be + V-ing. ✅ Others: "must to be" ✗, "have knew" ✗, "been knew" ✗.

opts: They're different modals with different grammar
"May" is more formal; "might" is slightly less certain in some contexts; both express possibility
questions.correct: "May" is more formal; "might" is slightly less certain in some contexts; both express possibility
questions.hint: "May" = formal (academic, official). "Might" = slightly more tentative. Both = possibility. ✅

questions.text: "He ___ (be) in the meeting — his light is on and his coat is there."
questions.hint: Multiple pieces of evidence → strong deduction. "He MUST BE in the meeting." ✅

questions.text: "He must have been exhausted" vs "He must have been exhausting." — difference:
opts: "Must have been exhausted" = he felt exhausted; "must have been exhausting" = the experience was exhausting
questions.correct: "Must have been exhausted" = he felt exhausted; "must have been exhausting" = the experience was exhausting
questions.hint: "Must have been exhausted" (his state). "Must have been exhausting" (the activity was tiring). Different subjects/meanings. ✅

questions.text: "They can't have been doing it all year — the records only go back three months." — "can't have been doing" suggests:
opts: Near-certainty that an ongoing past action did NOT happen for the claimed period
questions.correct: Near-certainty that an ongoing past action did NOT happen for the claimed period
questions.hint: "can't have been + V-ing" = past continuous deduction (impossibility). Evidence (3-month records) contradicts the claim. ✅

questions.text: "She might be right." (50%) → New strong evidence arrives. Choose the stronger deduction:
questions.hint: As evidence strengthens, shift from "might be" (50%) to "must be" (95%). ✅
